outcome: Chess remains unsolved: no proof of the game-theoretic outcome of the starting position under perfect play exists as of September 2026, and no serious claim to the contrary has been made.
summary: The question of what the game-theoretic outcome of a perfectly played game of chess is (win for White, win for Black, or draw) remains completely open as of September 2026, with no change since the frozen revision. The Wikipedia 'Solving chess' article states plainly that no complete solution in either the strong or weak sense is known and none is expected soon; this has not changed since January 2024. The only concrete progress in the relevant area since 2024 is on endgame tablebases: Niklas Fiekas and Marc Bourzutschky released a partial 8-piece tablebase ('op1', covering positions with an opposing pawn pair) in a Lichess blog post dated 2026-02-07. This was produced by exhaustive retrograde analysis — brute-force backward computation from checkmate/known-win positions — not by any AI or machine-learning system; the blog post explicitly describes the method as retrograde analysis. Even setting the AI question aside, this does not count under §3.1: the question 'what is the outcome of a perfectly played game from the start' is an existence/answer-type question that is only advanced by an actual determination of that outcome, not by extending tablebase coverage deeper into the endgame space (analogous to the rule that record-extension does not advance an infinitude question). I also checked for any AI lab claims of having solved or nearly solved chess (e.g., DeepMind, OpenAI) — searches turned up only chess-playing performance milestones (e.g., OpenAI's o3 winning a 2025 Kaggle chess exhibition) and AI-for-chess-puzzle-generation research, none of which bears on the theoretical outcome question, and no retraction-worthy claims either. A tangential arXiv paper title ('Semi-Strongly solved: a New Definition Leading Computer to Perfect Gameplay', Takizawa, Nov 2024) initially looked relevant but on inspection concerns 6x6 Othello, not chess, and introduces a new solving-strength category rather than reporting any chess result — it is an unrelated problem under §3.1 and was excluded. Expert consensus that perfect play likely results in a draw is unchanged from the 19th century (Steinitz, 1889) and remains unproven. No change to record for this problem.
competing_reading: None of the material found is even arguably in scope; there is no close call here. The 8-piece tablebase work is the closest thing to 'progress' in the surrounding literature, but it neither touches nor could touch the starting-position outcome question under any reasonable reading, since full 8-piece and beyond tablebases are still vastly short of the 32-piece starting position, and tablebase completion for a fixed piece count is a different (bounded, decidable) question from the game's true value.
what_would_settle_it: A weak solution of chess from the initial position (a proof, verified by experts, establishing the game's value as win/loss/draw with a strategy securing that outcome against any opposition) would resolve this. Short of that, nothing currently on the horizon (given 10^40+ legal positions) moves this question; a claimed breakthrough would need independent expert verification given the field's history of unverified claims.
